entry.title: Five Lines to Any Hardware - Inside huggingface/accelerate

link.title: Five Lines to Any Hardware - Inside huggingface/accelerate

entry.content:
Every PyTorch practitioner eventually hits the same wall: the training loop that ran beautifully on a laptop needs distributed ranks, gradient synchronization, loss scaling, and device juggling the moment it meets real hardware, and the boilerplate for all of that dwarfs the actual science. huggingface/accelerate, the Apache-2.0 library under most modern Hugging Face training stacks, takes a different path from the monolithic trainer frameworks: it refuses to own your loop. You keep writing the while-loop you already understand, add five lines, and the same script runs on one CPU, eight GPUs, a TPU pod, or any of a growing zoo of accelerators, with fp8, fp16, or bf16 mixed precision handled underneath. The library is deliberately thin in philosophy and decidedly not thin in engineering, which is exactly what makes its source worth reading. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The repository splits cleanly into four layers. The command-line layer gives you accelerate config, a questionnaire that saves your hardware setup, and accelerate launch, a 1338-line launcher that knows how to start single or multi-node runs without you memorizing torch.distributed.run flags. The state layer, state.py at 1181 lines, holds three singletons that discover the environment once and share it everywhere. The core layer is accelerator.py, 3738 lines around a single Accelerator class whose prepare method wraps whatever you hand it. And the device layer is a hook system: AlignDevicesHook and its offloading cousins move pieces of models between CPU, disk, and accelerator memory at execution time, the machinery that lets Transformers load a 30B model on a single consumer card. Reading the overview from left to right traces a request from the terminal, through environment detection, into the core, and down into the hooks that physically move tensors.

Overview of Accelerate: the CLI launches scripts that read shared state singletons, the Accelerator wraps training objects in one call, and the hook system performs device placement and offloading.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • accelerate config is a 70-line command that walks you through hardware questions and writes a reusable default_config.yaml.
  • accelerate launch is the 1338-line CLI that translates that config into worker processes, env vars, and backend-specific arguments.
  • launchers.py is the 285-line fallback that starts distributed runs from inside a plain script or notebook when no launcher process exists.
  • state.py is the source of truth: PartialState at line 123, AcceleratorState at 877, and GradientState at 1240 resolve the environment exactly once per process.
  • Accelerator is the class at line 184 that your script imports, holding prepare, backward, logging, and checkpoint methods.
  • prepare is the one call, at line 1414, that adapts a model, data loaders, optimizer, and scheduler to the current setup.
  • hooks.py is the placement engine, from the 58-line ModelHook base to AlignDevicesHook at line 242 and CpuOffload at 721.
  • big_modeling.py is the public toolkit for huge weights: init_empty_weights, cpu_offload, disk_offload, and dispatch_model.

Why You Need This

The README sells the library with a diff, and the diff is honest. You add the import, construct an Accelerator, replace the device literal with accelerator.device, wrap your model, optimizer, and dataloader in prepare, and swap loss.backward for accelerator.backward. Five edited lines. The same file then runs unchanged on a single GPU, a multi-GPU node, or a TPU, with mixed precision selected by config instead of code edits. A second variant in the README goes further: hand device placement to the library entirely and delete the to(device) calls, letting prepare move data and modules for you. This is a genuinely different contract from trainer frameworks; nothing is taken away, which is why so many projects adopt it incrementally rather than as a rewrite.

The hardware coverage in state.py is the part outsiders underestimate. The detection logic recognizes MULTI_GPU and XLA, of course, but also MULTI_MLU, MULTI_SDAA, MULTI_MUSA, MULTI_NPU, MULTI_HPU, MULTI_XPU, and MULTI_NEURON, falling back to MULTI_CPU or plain NO when nothing exotic is present. That list is the footprint of real-world inference and training hardware across vendors, and Accelerate is one of the few libraries that normalizes all of it behind one Accelerator object. Your loop never learns which accelerator it is on; the state singletons do, once, at import time, through a thread-local store that keeps parallel test runs from colliding.

The third reason is the big-model side, which has quietly become infrastructure for the entire ecosystem. init_empty_weights at line 62 of big_modeling.py builds a model on the meta device so a 70B parameter architecture costs kilobytes of RAM until weights arrive. dispatch_model at line 315 then assigns each layer to a device, and load_checkpoint_and_dispatch at line 524 streams the checkpoint in and wires it up. The CpuOffload hook, at line 721 of hooks.py, streams weights to the accelerator just before each forward and discards them after, trading a little latency for a lot of memory. If you have ever loaded a model larger than your GPU, you have run this code path.

Detail view: the launch commands, every major Accelerator method with its line number, the three state singletons and the device enum, the hook classes, and the big-model plus wrapper utilities.

The state layer rewards a close look because everything else leans on it. PartialState, at line 123 of state.py, is usable in any script with or without the Accelerator: it reads the environment variables that a launcher exported, queries the process group, and exposes device and distributed_type. AcceleratorState, at line 877, is the shared instance that all Accelerator objects in one process agree on, which is how a notebook can construct two Accelerators without starting two process groups. GradientState, at line 1240, is the smallest and most subtle: it tracks whether the current micro-batch is inside a no_sync window so that gradient accumulation skips process-group reductions on all but the last step. The AcceleratedOptimizer wrapper in optimizer.py, at line 38, consults that state before letting a step through, which is how accumulation works without touching your loop.

prepare itself is a dispatcher with seventeen special cases. The model path, prepare_model at line 1769, casts dtypes, attaches hooks, and handles compile and quantization integration; prepare_data_loader at line 2684 builds a DataLoaderShard whose BatchSamplerShard, at line 110 of data_loader.py, splits batches evenly and pads uneven tails so ranks never hang waiting for a straggler batch; prepare_optimizer and prepare_scheduler, at lines 2743 and 2787, wrap into the gated AcceleratedOptimizer and AcceleratedScheduler at line 25 of scheduler.py. The 1295-line data_loader.py module also contributes SeedableRandomSampler at line 73, which makes random data order reproducible across ranks, and DataLoaderDispatcher at line 726 for setups where the data loader lives on one process and steps happen elsewhere.

The backward path is where precision engineering hides. accelerator.backward at line 2828 routes through the native accelerator scaler for fp16, the native bf16 path, or fp8 handling depending on configuration, then calls the underlying loss.backward with the right arguments. clip_grad_norm_ at line 2988 knows to unscale gradients before measuring norms, a detail many hand-rolled loops get wrong. On the metrics side, gather_for_metrics at line 3108 collects tensors from every rank and drops the padding that the even-batch sharding introduced, so your accuracy numbers are computed on real samples only. save_state at line 3624 and load_state at 3790 round-trip the entire setup, model, optimizer, schedulers, random states, and registration order included, which is what makes interrupted distributed runs resumable at all.

The hook system is the architectural trick that keeps all of this composable. ModelHook at line 58 of hooks.py is a tiny class that wraps a module’s forward and detach; add_hook_to_module at line 147 attaches one to any nn.Module by overriding its forward, and SequentialHook at 116 chains them. AlignDevicesHook at line 242 is the workhorse: on entry it casts and moves a module’s parameters and buffers to its execution device, runs the wrapped forward, and optionally offloads again on exit. attach_align_device_hook_on_blocks at line 587 applies it recursively to every block of a model, which is precisely how dispatch_model implements its device map. The 742-line big_modeling.py module is just the public face of this machinery, and utils/modeling.py, at 1942 lines, supplies the weight-loading and offload-store utilities underneath, while utils/operations.py, at 808 lines, converts tensor sends, pads, and reductions into their distributed equivalents.

From Install to a Launched Run

Configure once, then launch:

pip install accelerate

accelerate config          # answer questions about GPU count, precision, distributed setup
accelerate launch train.py # starts single or multi-GPU training with zero code flags

Inside train.py, the whole integration is the five-line diff from the README:

# from accelerate import Accelerator
# accelerator = Accelerator()
# device = accelerator.device
# model, optimizer, data = accelerator.prepare(model, optimizer, data)
# accelerator.backward(loss)

The first two commands pick up default_config.yaml written by the questionnaire, so teammates and CI machines share one launch recipe instead of a wiki page of torchrun flags.

Honest limits: Accelerate deliberately does not schedule training for you, so learning-rate policy, evaluation cadence, and checkpoint rotation remain your loop’s job, and projects that want those managed graduate to Trainer or TRL on top. The five-line promise holds for standard loops, but exotic patterns such as two optimizers with different accumulation schedules or hand-written process-group collectives still leak distributed concepts through the abstraction. The hook-based offloading trades latency for memory and is tuned for inference-shaped workloads, not every training shape. And the device zoo, impressive as the enum is, means the long tail of accelerators gets community-tested coverage rather than vendor-certified support. What the source shows, line after line, is an unusual discipline: a library that grew to underpin an ecosystem while refusing to take your training loop hostage.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of huggingface/accelerate: how one 3738-line Accelerator class, three state singletons, and a hook system for device placement turn a raw PyTorch training loop into multi-GPU, TPU, and mixed-precision code.

entry.title: One Booster, Every Parallelism - Inside hpcaitech/ColossalAI

link.title: One Booster, Every Parallelism - Inside hpcaitech/ColossalAI

entry.content:
Training a modern large model is a combinatorics problem disguised as a systems problem: data parallel or tensor parallel or stage parallel, optimizer states on GPU or CPU, activations recomputed or offloaded, and every combination trades memory against throughput differently. hpcaitech/ColossalAI, the Apache-2.0 project from HPC-AI Technology, is one of the most complete open answers: a single training facade called Booster, behind which a family of plugins can turn on any mix of data, tensor, and stage parallelism, ZeRO-style optimizer sharding, chunk-based CPU offloading, FP8 mixed precision, and mixture-of-experts, all without rewriting the model. The project’s own README benchmark is aggressive about it: a 70B Llama-like model at 811.79 TFLOPS per GPU on 16 H200s with a hybrid layout, and B200 nodes beating H200 by 50 to 70 percent on throughput. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The architecture is a stack of increasingly clever wrappers. At the top sits Booster, a facade class whose boost method accepts any model, optimizer, and plugin and returns wrapped versions that behave like the originals. Plugins decide everything: the flagship HybridParallelPlugin composes data, tensor, and stage parallelism with three optimizer tiers, while GeminiPlugin brings the chunked memory system that migrates parameters between GPU and CPU in large blocks. Underneath, the Shardformer rewrites transformer architectures module by module for tensor parallel execution, guided by per-model policy files, and the DTensor layout engine supplies the distributed math. Around the core live an inference system with its own KV cache and server, Triton kernels for attention primitives, and MoE operations. Reading the overview from left to right follows one training step from the facade, through plugin selection, into the memory and sharding machinery.

Overview of ColossalAI: the Booster facade delegates to a plugin family, Gemini chunks migrate parameter memory, and the Shardformer plus DTensor engine handles tensor-parallel surgery.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Booster is the facade at line 33: boost, backward, no_sync, LoRA helpers, and model, optimizer, and scheduler save and load all route through it.
  • colossalai.initialize is the 157-line boot sequence that builds the parallel context from launcher environment variables.
  • Plugin is the 74-line contract every parallel strategy implements, deciding how models, optimizers, and dataloaders get wrapped.
  • HybridParallelPlugin is the flagship at line 929, composing data, tensor, and stage parallelism with naive, AMP, and ZeRO optimizer tiers.
  • GeminiDDP is the 875-line memory wrapper that keeps parameters in chunks which migrate on demand.
  • ChunkManager plus chunk.py pack parameters and optimizer states into large, pinned, movable memory blocks.
  • LowLevelZeroOptimizer partitions gradients and optimizer states across the data-parallel group, ZeRO stage 1 and 2 style.
  • Shardformer is the 43-line engine that, given a policy file such as the 487-line LlamaPolicy, splits a transformer for tensor parallel training.

Why You Need This

The benchmark table in the README is the honest sales pitch, and it is worth reading closely. On 8 H200 GPUs training a 7B Llama-like model with ZeRO-2 data parallelism, Colossal-AI reports 17.13 samples per second at 534.18 TFLOPS per GPU. Switch to a 70B model on 16 H200s with the same ZeRO setup and it holds 3.27 samples per second at 469.1 TFLOPS. The hybrid layouts are where it gets interesting: zero1 plus tensor-parallel-2 plus 4-way stage splitting reaches 805.69 TFLOPS per GPU on 8 B200s for the 7B model and 811.79 on 16 H200s for the 70B, with peak memory around 100GB per card. The project’s headline numbers, 50 percent higher throughput for the 7B and over 70 percent for the 70B when moving to B200, are all measured with these in-repo configurations, and the benchmark scripts sit in the examples tree for verification.

The second reason is architectural: Booster is one of the cleanest plugin systems in the training-framework space. The facade at line 33 of booster.py exposes about thirty public methods, from boost at line 126 through backward at 175, load_model at 291, save_model at 315, optimizer save and load at 352 and 372, and LoRA helpers enable_lora at 240 and save_lora_as_pretrained at 418. Every one of those delegates to the active plugin, which means the difference between pure data parallel, FSDP, ZeRO, Gemini offloading, or full 3D parallelism is a config object, not a code change. A 44-line accelerator shim abstracts the hardware calls underneath, and the 157-line initialize module wires the parallel context from the launcher environment before any of it runs.

The third reason is the memory science. Gemini, the chunked memory system, is Colossal-AI’s answer to the question of what to do when parameters, gradients, and optimizer states do not fit: pack them into large chunks rather than moving tensors one by one. chunk.py, at 560 lines, implements a chunk as a contiguous memory region with a GPU window and a pinned CPU shard, and manager.py, at 270 lines, allocates and tracks them. A placement policy module, 240 lines, decides what lives where, and gemini_hook.py moves data at the four boundaries of a training step: before and after forward, before and after backward. The companion LowLevelZeroOptimizer partitions gradients through a bookkeeping layer of bucket and gradient stores, so stage 1 and 2 sharding work with asynchronous reduction hooks. Reading these files is a graduate course in memory management.

Detail view: the Booster facade and its entry methods, the full plugin family, the Gemini chunk machinery from manager to hooks, the Shardformer stack, and the MoE, FP8, and kernel support layer.

The HybridParallelPlugin file is where the composition happens, and its class layout tells the story. HybridParallelModule, at line 60 of hybrid_parallel_plugin.py, is the model wrapper that knows about tensor-parallel groups and stage boundaries; HybridParallelNaiveOptimizer at line 279 is the plain data-parallel path; HybridParallelAMPOptimizer at line 491 adds fp16 and bf16 loss scaling; and HybridParallelZeroOptimizer at line 667 extends the LowLevelZeroOptimizer so that ZeRO sharding works on top of the other two parallel axes simultaneously. The plugin itself, at line 929, extends the stage-parallel plugin base, which is why the same config can express the zero1-plus-TP2-plus-4-way-stage layout from the benchmark table. A separate MoE hybrid variant exists for expert models, and there are baseline torch DDP and FSDP plugins for apples-to-apples comparisons. The facade covers the interaction patterns a multi-axis run actually needs: Booster.no_sync at line 223 creates accumulation windows where gradients skip cross-rank reduction, and the scheduler save and load methods at lines 400 and 409 round-trip learning-rate state alongside the optimizer, so a resumed 3D run restarts warm rather than cold.

The project’s ecosystem is evidence the abstraction survives contact with real workloads. Open-Sora, the team’s video-generation effort, trains its diffusion transformers on this stack; ColossalChat used it for the full RLHF sequence on chat models; Colossal-LLaMA-2 demonstrated domain-specific fine-tuning in a half-day of training on rented hardware; and a February 2025 guide walked through fine-tuning DeepSeek’s 671B-parameter model with the upgraded toolchain. Those projects exercise very different corners of the plugin matrix, video generation favoring activation-heavy stage splits, RLHF favoring the inference side, and 671B-scale tuning leaning entirely on the chunked memory system. A library that hosts all four under one facade has put its abstraction where the workloads are.

The Shardformer is the component outsiders should study first, because tensor parallelism is usually the most painful part to implement by hand. The engine, shardformer.py, is only 43 lines: it takes a model, a ShardConfig of 110 lines of flags, and a policy, then performs the module surgery. The policies folder holds one file per architecture, and LlamaPolicy at 487 lines shows the pattern: each attention, MLP, and normalization sublayer is annotated with the sharding spec it should receive, plus optimizations like fused kernels where the groups allow. The DTensor engine underneath, in the d_tensor package with api, comm_spec, sharding_spec, and layout_converter modules, computes and converts the distributed layouts so that a matrix split four ways reduces correctly. Getting this wrong produces silent divergence; the policy files are effectively reviewed recipes.

The support layer rounds out the picture. The quantization package ships fp8.py and fp8_hook.py, the one-line FP8 mixed-precision integration the project blog credits with cutting training cost by up to 30 percent, plus bitsandbytes integration in bnb.py. The kernel package holds Triton implementations of the primitives large models need, from rms_layernorm and fused rotary embeddings to flash decoding and KV cache copy routines. The inference package is a serving system of its own, with core, executor, kv_cache, and server subpackages, and the auto_parallel module carries the compiler side: passes, checkpoint planning, offload planning, and profilers that reason about sharding choices before you commit them. The mixture-of-experts support lives in a compact _operation module plus its plugin variant, enough to see how experts are dispatched across ranks.

From Install to a Launched Run

The Llama example’s Gemini benchmark script shows the launcher in real form:

pip install colossalai
git clone https://github.com/hpcaitech/ColossalAI
cd ColossalAI/examples/language/llama

# one command starts 8 workers and applies the Gemini chunked-memory config
colossalai run --nproc_per_node 8 --hostfile hosts.txt benchmark.py -g -x -b 16

Inside the training script, the only structural change is the Booster pattern: construct a plugin, call booster.boost(model, optimizer), and train through booster.backward instead of loss.backward. Everything else, from chunk migration to gradient bucketing, happens inside the wrappers.

Honest limits: Colossal-AI’s breadth is also its operating cost. The plugin matrix multiplies, and exotic combinations such as MoE plus stage parallelism plus FP8 carry compatibility caveats that only the test suite fully maps. The custom kernels and CUDA extensions mean installation is heavier than a pure-Python library, with build toolchains that matter on older driver stacks. The headline benchmark numbers come from the project’s own hardware and scripts; reproducing 800-plus TFLOPS per GPU requires the exact H200 or B200 configurations listed. And the Gemini chunk system, while elegant, tunes through several interacting knobs, chunk size and placement policy chief among them, that reward experimentation. What the source demonstrates is a serious systems argument: parallelism strategies are composable objects, and a good facade makes the combinatorics navigable.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of hpcaitech/ColossalAI: how the Booster facade, a plugin family spanning 3D parallelism and ZeRO, chunk-based Gemini memory, and the Shardformer make large model training fit on the hardware you have.

entry.title: Train 0.19 Percent of the Model - Inside huggingface/peft

link.title: Train 0.19 Percent of the Model - Inside huggingface/peft

entry.content:
Full fine-tuning is the luxury the rest of us cannot afford. A 12B-parameter model in fp16 needs around 47GB of GPU memory before the optimizer even gets its share, which is why so many promising fine-tuning projects died the moment someone loaded the weights. huggingface/peft, the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning library, is the industry’s standard answer: freeze the backbone, learn a tiny set of extra weights instead, and ship checkpoints measured in megabytes. The Apache-2.0 repository has grown into a zoo of 46 tuner methods, from LoRA and DoRA through prompt tuning, IA3, VeRA, and X-LoRA, all sharing one injection framework and one checkpoint format. It is the library underneath QLoRA training jobs, TRL reinforcement-learning runs, and countless adapter swaps on the Hub. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The codebase is organized with unusual discipline for something this dynamic. The public entry point is a single function, get_peft_model, in an 81-line dispatch module that maps a config object to a tuner class through registries that methods register themselves into. The wrapper layer, peft_model.py, runs 3242 lines and adds six task-specific subclasses on top of the base PeftModel. Underneath, every tuner follows the same contract defined in tuners_utils.py: walk the model, find target modules, replace them with wrapped layers. The LoRA implementation is the reference citizen, with a 2429-line layer file that carries the full math of low-rank adaptation, including rank-stabilized scaling, per-layer rank patterns, DoRA magnitude vectors, and merge and unmerge surgery on quantized weights. Reading the overview from left to right shows a clean funnel: two entry functions, a registry, one big wrapper family, and one tuner contract.

Overview of PEFT: two entry functions share a registry of tuner classes, PeftModel and its six task subclasses wrap the result, and the LoRA tuner demonstrates the layer contract that all 46 methods follow.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • get_peft_model is the front door: it resolves a config such as LoraConfig into a tuner, injects the adapters, and hands back a PeftModel.
  • inject_adapter_in_model is the lower-level sibling that mutates your model in place and returns the same object, for people who already have their own wrapper.
  • register_peft_method is how the 46 methods plug in: each tuner registers its config class, tuner class, and checkpoint prefix into shared tables.
  • PeftModel is the base wrapper at line 140, carrying adapter add, load, set, and delete operations plus save_pretrained and generate.
  • six task subclasses specialize forward and generate for causal LM, seq2seq, classification, token classification, question answering, and feature extraction.
  • LoraModel is the reference tuner: it walks named_modules and swaps every target for a LoRA-wrapped copy, honoring per-key rank and alpha patterns.
  • LoraLayer holds the math: per-adapter rank, the A and B matrices, the alpha-over-r scaling, and the merge code that folds adapters into base weights.
  • save_and_load.py is why checkpoints stay tiny: it filters the state dict down to adapter weights only, keyed by adapter name.

Why You Need This

The README opens with a table that explains the entire value proposition in three rows. On an A100 80GB GPU, full fine-tuning of bigscience/T0_3B consumes 47.14GB of GPU memory; the same model with LoRA needs 14.4GB; LoRA plus DeepSpeed CPU offloading brings it to 9.8GB. Move up to the 12B mt0-xxl and full fine-tuning runs out of memory entirely, while LoRA fits at 56GB and offloaded LoRA at 22GB. The bloomz-7b1 numbers follow the same shape. Quality holds up too: on the twitter_complaints task, the LoRA-trained T0 scores 0.863 against a Flan-T5 baseline of 0.892 and a crowdsourced human baseline of 0.897.

Storage is the second argument, and it is the one that changed how people share models. A full T0_3B checkpoint is 11GB; the LoRA adapter for the same model is 19MB, roughly a 500-fold reduction. That ratio is what makes the adapter economy on the Hugging Face Hub possible: one frozen backbone on disk, hundreds of task adapters beside it, each a few megabytes. The library leans into this with load_adapter and set_adapter on PeftModel, so a serving process can hot-swap personalities without reloading weights, and with create_or_update_model_card, which writes a metadata card into every checkpoint folder it saves.

The third argument is the quantization story that became QLoRA. The LoRA tuner ships dedicated wrapper files for bitsandbytes 4-bit and 8-bit layers, plus GPTQ, AQLM, AWQ, HQQ, and EETQ formats, each teaching the adapter how to dequantize, add the low-rank update, and merge back without ever materializing the full fp16 weight. The README points to a recipe that fine-tunes meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-hf on a 16GB consumer GPU using exactly this path. If you have ever wondered what actually happens between “load_in_4bit” and a trainable layer, this is the code that answers it.

Detail view: the entry and registry layer, the PeftModel family with its adapter lifecycle, the LoRA internals from config to scaling to merge, and the quantized variants plus checkpoint format.

Start at the entry points. get_peft_model, defined at line 105 of mapping_func.py, and inject_adapter_in_model, at line 47 of mapping.py, both depend on tables that start empty: PEFT_TYPE_TO_CONFIG_MAPPING, PEFT_TYPE_TO_TUNER_MAPPING, and friends are dicts in mapping.py that register_peft_method fills at import time. That registration pattern is why the library can carry 46 methods without a single if-chain in its dispatch code; adding a tuner means adding a folder and a registration call, never touching the front door. The injection function does enforce a few hard rules, rejecting prompt-learning methods and tuners with shared state, since those need the full PeftModel wrapper rather than bare mutation.

PeftModel, at line 140 of peft_model.py, is where the wrapper personality lives. Its constructor branches on whether the config is prompt-learning: prompt methods keep the raw model and hang a prompt encoder off it, while everything else instantiates the tuner class from the registry, which returns the model with wrapped layers inside. After wrapping it casts adapter dtypes, prepares gradient checkpointing, and forces pretraining_tp to 1 to avoid numerical surprises from tensor-simulation settings. The adapter lifecycle is explicit and worth knowing for serving: add_adapter at line 1109, load_adapter at 1515, set_adapter at 1705, and delete_adapter at 1190. Meanwhile get_nb_trainable_parameters at line 953 powers print_trainable_parameters, the call that prints the famous line from the README quickstart: 3,686,400 trainable parameters out of 3,089,625,088 total, or 0.1193 percent, for a Qwen2.5-3B model with rank 16.

The LoRA internals repay a slow read. LoraLayer, at line 108 of layer.py, keeps per-adapter dicts of rank, the A and B matrices, dropout, and scaling, so multiple adapters coexist in one layer. In update_layer, lora_A is created as a plain nn.Linear from in_features down to rank r, and lora_B as an nn.Linear from r back up to out_features; A gets kaiming-uniform initialization while B starts at zero, which is the trick that keeps the initial adapter output silent. The scaling factor is lora_alpha divided by r at line 281, or alpha over the square root of r when use_rslora is set, following the rank-stabilized recipe. Forward passes then compute base_layer(x) plus the scaled B-times-A projection, and the merge code computes the delta weight as exactly that product so adapters can be folded into the base matrix and later unfolded without loss.

The traversal side is LoraModel, at line 165 of model.py. Its _create_and_replace at line 294 resolves per-key overrides first: rank_pattern and alpha_pattern are dicts of regex-to-value, looked up with get_pattern_key against the current module name, so you can ask for rank 64 on attention projections and rank 8 everywhere else in one config. It then passes r, alpha, and quantization flags into _create_new_module at line 499, which picks the right wrapper class for the target, including the quantized variants. If the target is already a LoRA layer, it simply adds another adapter to it, which is how multi-adapter layers work. The config file itself is a study in accretion: LoraConfig at line 514 is surrounded by companion configs for runtime options, VeRA, LoftQ, ARROW, EVA, CorDA, and more, each representing a research refinement the community adopted.

Persistence is the quiet achievement. get_peft_model_state_dict at line 148 of save_and_load.py extracts only adapter weights, remaps their names into the checkpoint format, and set_peft_model_state_dict at line 549 reverses the process on load, with load_peft_weights at 702 handling the remote fetch from the Hub. The artifact is two files, adapter_model.safetensors and adapter_config.json, the name defined in constants.py at line 400. Because every method uses the same keys, a checkpoint carries its own config and can be loaded years later without the original training script. For debugging, TunerLayerStatus and TunerModelStatus at lines 3358 and 3488 print per-layer tables of what is wrapped where, and mixed_model.py, at 397 lines, composes several methods into one model for the rare cases where LoRA plus prompt tuning is genuinely the answer.

From Install to a Trained Adapter

The quickstart from the README trains a rank-16 LoRA adapter on a 3B model in a few lines:

pip install peft

python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from peft import LoraConfig, TaskType, get_peft_model

device = torch.accelerator.current_accelerator().type if hasattr(torch, "accelerator") else "cuda"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct", device_map=device)
peft_config = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, task_type=TaskType.CAUSAL_LM)
model = get_peft_model(model, peft_config)
model.print_trainable_parameters()
# trainable params: 3,686,400 || all params: 3,089,625,088 || trainable%: 0.1193

# train with your favorite Trainer, then:
model.save_pretrained("qwen2.5-3b-lora")
PY

Loading for inference mirrors it: rebuild the base model, then PeftModel.from_pretrained(model, “qwen2.5-3b-lora”) reattaches the adapter and you can generate immediately.

Honest limits: PEFT is a wrapper library, not a trainer, so you still bring Transformers, Accelerate, or TRL for the training loop, and the README’s own examples lean on those siblings for scheduling and distributed setup. Prompt-learning methods and tuners with shared state cannot use the in-place injection API, a restriction the code states rather than hides. The 46-method zoo is a strength and a hazard: method quality varies by task and model, and the README is candid that numbers like the 0.863 accuracy come from an unoptimized configuration you can probably beat with tuning. Merging adapters into base weights is lossless only when you control the dtype math, and on quantized backbones the merge path is necessarily heavier. None of that diminishes the core result this repository proves line by line: for a very large class of adaptation problems, the 99.88 percent of the model you were about to train did not need training at all.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of huggingface/peft: how 46 adapter methods, a 3242-line PeftModel shell, and per-layer LoRA scaling math let you fine-tune a 3B-parameter LLM by training less than one percent of its weights.

entry.title: Your Science, Their Engineering - Inside Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning

link.title: Your Science, Their Engineering - Inside Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning

entry.content:
Every PyTorch project eventually grows the same skeleton: a training function that moves batches to the device, zeroes gradients, calls backward, clips gradients, steps the optimizer, logs metrics, validates at intervals, saves checkpoints, and then gets rewritten when someone says the words multi-GPU or mixed precision. Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning, the Apache-2.0 repository behind the packages you install as lightning and pytorch-lightning, is that skeleton extracted into a framework, tested by an enormous test suite, and scaled to everything from a laptop CPU to multi-node clusters. The project’s README puts the value proposition in one line: if PyTorch is JavaScript, PyTorch Lightning is ReactJS or NextJS. You write the model and the science; the framework owns the engineering around it. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The repository is a monorepo serving two packages at once. The src/lightning/pytorch tree holds the high-level Trainer experience; the src/lightning/fabric tree holds Fabric, a thinner expert API that gives you explicit control over devices, precision, and distribution without owning your loop. Both sit on the exact same strategy layer, and a small bridge class inside core/module.py even lets Fabric strategies power the full Trainer. Around these live a loop engine that decomposes training into nestable, restartable pieces, a connector that translates constructor flags into accelerator and device decisions, and a callback system with twenty pluggable behaviors from checkpointing to learning-rate finding. Reading the overview from left to right walks one fit call from the facade, through the loops, down into the hardware layer.

Overview of pytorch-lightning: the Trainer facade resolves hardware through the accelerator connector, the loop engine drives your LightningModule, and a Strategy family from single device to DeepSpeed handles the distributed math, with Fabric sharing the same layer.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Trainer is the facade at line 89 of a 1797-line file, exposing fit at line 533, validate at 647, test at 765, and predict at 884, all funneling into one run path.
  • LightningModule is the user contract at line 92 of an 1849-line file: training_step at 711, configure_optimizers at 991, and the rank-aware log method at 381.
  • FitLoop is the outer loop at line 59 of 565 lines, nesting epoch loops while tracking progress and checkpointing its own reload state.
  • The training epoch loop at line 51 of 588 lines iterates batches, manages accumulation windows, and routes each one to optimization or evaluation.
  • Automatic optimization is a 329-line driver at line 153 whose Closure at line 92 caches the training-step result so backward and optimizer stepping can be replayed safely.
  • Strategy is the 649-line base contract at line 47; DDPStrategy at line 68 and DeepSpeedStrategy at line 76 of 945 lines are two of its many heirs.
  • The accelerator connector is a 593-line resolver at line 74 that turns constructor flags into a concrete accelerator, device set, and precision plugin.
  • Fabric is the expert API at line 86 of 1260 lines, exposing explicit setup, launch, backward, and step methods over the same strategy layer through a shared 580-line connector.

Why You Need This

The honest answer starts with repetition. A serious PyTorch project does not need three lines to train; it needs hundreds of lines that have nothing to do with the model: device plumbing, gradient accumulation, distributed process groups, precision handling, checkpoint formats, resumption logic, and logging glue. Each of these is easy to write once and painful to maintain across every experiment, and each becomes a bug farm the moment you move from one GPU to eight. Lightning takes that entire category of code and owns it in one audited place, so the diff between your CPU experiment and your cluster run becomes a constructor argument instead of a refactor.

The second reason is scale without rewrites. Because every distributed concern lives behind the Strategy interface, the same LightningModule you debug on a single device runs under DDP, FSDP, DeepSpeed, model parallel, or TPU execution without touching your model code. The framework decides how tensors move, which processes run which code, and how the optimizer states are sharded. When a new parallel scheme appears, the library adds a strategy; your code does not change. That decoupling is why the framework survived the industry’s rapid shifts from DDP to ZeRO-style sharding to fully sharded data parallel approaches over just a few years.

The third reason is the safety net under research code. The sanity check that runs a few validation batches before training starts catches broken dataloaders in seconds instead of after an epoch. The checkpoint system saves model, optimizer, and loop state together, so a crashed run resumes mid-epoch rather than mid-apology. Callbacks like ModelCheckpoint and EarlyStopping watch metrics and act on them, and the Tuner can find a learning rate and a batch size before you waste a week on both. These are unglamorous features, and they are exactly the ones that decide whether a project ships.

The detailed map: Trainer entry points converge on one run path, the loop engine decomposes into fit, epoch, evaluation, and prediction loops with an automatic optimization driver, the strategy family implements the hardware contract, and Fabric plus the Tuner share the same plumbing.

Follow one call to trainer.fit and the design snaps into focus. The fit method at line 533 validates its arguments, records that the function stage is fitting through the enums in states.py (RunningStage at line 44, TrainerState at 75), and calls _run at line 1008. That setup method is where the accelerator connector’s decisions become real: the strategy is instantiated and set up, loggers and callbacks get attached, and the environment is checked. Then _run_stage at line 1121 dispatches: training goes to the fit loop, evaluation to the shared evaluation loop. Before any real training, _run_sanity_check at line 1138 runs two validation batches by default, a tiny preflight that has saved countless runs from silently broken data.

The loop engine is the most instructive part. FitLoop owns epochs; the _TrainingEpochLoop owns batches and decides, per batch, whether this step belongs to automatic or manual optimization. Under automatic optimization, the Closure at line 92 wraps your training_step call, stores the result in a ClosureResult, and hands a replayable object to the strategy’s optimizer step. That indirection is what lets the framework accumulate gradients across batches, clip them, and step the right optimizer on the right boundary, including when a scheduler needs the closure at step time. Manual optimization flips the contract: override backward at line 1121 and optimizer_step at line 1354 on your LightningModule and the driver steps aside, which is how GAN-style alternating updates are expressed.

The strategy layer is where hardware stops being your problem. The Strategy base defines setup, model and optimizer wiring, backward, optimizer step, and the distributed operations, plus a _ForwardRedirection class at line 602 that keeps nn.Module hooks alive when forward calls must be re-routed. DDPStrategy wraps torch.distributed with launcher support for subprocess and notebook spawns, DeepSpeedStrategy bridges Microsoft’s ZeRO stages and CPU offloading, and FSDP and model parallel strategies cover sharded and layer-split execution. Even checkpoint saving routes through the strategy: trainer.save_checkpoint at line 1450 delegates so that each parallel scheme persists exactly what it needs to restore itself.

Fabric is the same machinery with the scaffolding stripped off. Instead of a Trainer owning the loop, Fabric gives you about a dozen explicit calls: setup the module and optimizers, launch the processes, call backward and step yourself. It shares the strategy layer through the same connector that powers the Trainer, and the _TrainerFabricShim at line 1835 of module.py is the bridge that lets Fabric strategies serve full Trainer runs. The Tuner at line 25 rounds out the toolbox with lr find and batch size scaling. And migration is handled by stub packages: the src/pytorch_lightning directory contains only metadata files that re-export the lightning namespace, so old imports keep working while the monorepo carries both eras.

From Install to Trained Model

The README’s promise is that organized PyTorch needs almost no ceremony:

pip install lightning
pip install torchvision
python main.py

And the smallest meaningful program is a LightningModule plus a Trainer, straight from the repository’s quick start:

import torch, torch.nn as nn, torch.utils.data as data, torchvision as tv
import torch.nn.functional as F
import lightning as L

class LitAutoEncoder(L.LightningModule):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(28 * 28, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 3))
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(3, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 28 * 28))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.encoder(x)

    def training_step(self, batch, batch_idx):
        x, _ = batch
        x = x.view(x.size(0), -1)
        z = self.encoder(x)
        x_hat = self.decoder(z)
        loss = F.mse_loss(x_hat, x)
        self.log("train_loss", loss)
        return loss

    def configure_optimizers(self):
        return torch.optim.Adam(self.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

dataset = tv.datasets.MNIST(".", download=True, transform=tv.transforms.ToTensor())
train, val = data.random_split(dataset, [55000, 5000])

autoencoder = LitAutoEncoder()
trainer = L.Trainer()
trainer.fit(autoencoder, data.DataLoader(train), data.DataLoader(val))

That program runs unchanged on a GPU box with the DDP strategy enabled, accumulates gradients with a flag, resumes from a checkpoint with another, and swaps optimizers’ precision with a third. The science stayed in the class; the engineering moved into the framework.

Honest limits: the abstraction has real weight. Debugging a training bug means learning where your code ends and the loop engine begins, and the hook ordering has enough surface area that newcomers occasionally fight the framework instead of the bug. The rename from pytorch-lightning to lightning left two import namespaces and a long deprecation trail. Expert users who want tight control often graduate to Fabric, which is both a feature and an admission that the Trainer is not for everyone. And the loop engine, restartable as it is, still assumes batch-centric training; genuinely exotic schedules end up in manual optimization mode anyway. None of this dims the core achievement: this repository turned the world’s most repeated training boilerplate into a maintained, tested, hardware-portable foundation, which is why so much modern AI code starts with import lightning.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning: how the Trainer facade, the LightningModule contract, the loop engine, and a Strategy family from DDP to DeepSpeed turn raw PyTorch into scalable training, with Fabric as the expert escape hatch.

entry.title: One Framework, Four Kinds of Retrieval - Inside UKPLab/sentence-transformers

link.title: One Framework, Four Kinds of Retrieval - Inside UKPLab/sentence-transformers

entry.content:
In 2019, two researchers at the UKP Lab in TU Darmstadt published Sentence-BERT and open-sourced the code that made transformer embeddings practical for sentences. Six years later that codebase, UKPLab/sentence-transformers under the Apache-2.0 license and now maintained within Hugging Face, has grown into the framework behind more than fifteen thousand pretrained models on the Hub and a permanent fixture of the MTEB retrieval leaderboard. The current development line, version 6.2.0, is no longer just sentence embeddings: the same package now ships four model families, SentenceTransformer for dense embeddings, CrossEncoder for reranking, SparseEncoder for SPLADE-style sparse vectors, and MultiVectorEncoder for ColBERT-style late interaction, all behind one import and one training story. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The architecture earns its simplicity through a shared core. Every family inherits from a single BaseModel that is literally an nn.Sequential of modules: a Transformer input module loads any Hugging Face checkpoint, then pooling, projection, and normalization modules shape the output. Each family is a thin subclass that adds its own encode-style methods, its own trainer glue, and its own loss library, while saving, hub uploads, multimodal inputs, batching, and backend exports live once in the base. Reading the overview from left to right follows that story: four facades, one core, one training bridge, and a utility belt from similarity math to ONNX export.

Overview of sentence-transformers: four family facades extend one BaseModel core built from composable modules, the BaseTrainer bridges Hugging Face's Trainer, and utilities plus export backends round out the package.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SentenceTransformer is the flagship at line 38 of 1341 lines, with encode implemented at 753 and the similarity method at 1056.
  • CrossEncoder is the reranker at line 32 of 826 lines: predict at 450 scores text pairs, rank at 642 returns ordered passages.
  • SparseEncoder at line 30 of 1473 lines produces vocabulary-sized sparse vectors, with a static sparsity reporter at 1157.
  • MultiVectorEncoder at line 63 of 1623 lines emits one vector per token, scored by MaxSim at 977.
  • BaseModel is the shared core at line 66 of 2045 lines, with save_pretrained at 806 and push_to_hub at 950.
  • The Transformer module is the input module at line 644 that wraps any Hugging Face checkpoint, dispatching by Router at line 30 for non-text modalities.
  • BaseTrainer is the training bridge at line 89 of 1334 lines, extending the Hugging Face Trainer for all four families.
  • util/similarity.py is the math belt of 940 lines: cos_sim at 59, dot_score at 101, manhattan at 135, each with pairwise variants.

Why You Need This

Retrieval is not one algorithm, it is a menu of trade-offs, and this repository is the only mainstream library that puts the whole menu behind one API. Dense embeddings compress a sentence into one vector: fast to search, occasionally lossy. A CrossEncoder reads query and passage together and scores them jointly: accurate, too slow to run over a whole corpus, which is exactly why it exists as a reranker. Sparse vectors keep the vocabulary dimension, so matching is transparent and lexical. Late interaction keeps one vector per token and scores with MaxSim, trading storage for fine-grained matching. Learning all four from scratch means four codebases; here they are four classes with the same load, save, encode, and similarity conventions.

The second reason is the module system, which is genuinely compositional rather than nominally so. A model is a chain: put a Transformer at the front, append Pooling to turn tokens into one vector, optionally a Dense projection or Normalize at the end, save it, and the chain definition travels with the weights. Swap Pooling for a sparse pooling module and the same skeleton produces SPLADE vectors; swap the front for StaticEmbedding lookup tables and you get CPU-friendly models that the project blogs about running dramatically faster than attention-based ones. Because every module implements the same save and load contract at the Module base class, custom research modules slot into pretrained models without forks.

The third reason is the training story, which is where most embedding projects stall. The library ships roughly twenty-eight embedding loss functions, from MultipleNegativesRankingLoss to cached variants that grow batch sizes to thousands of negatives, plus a dozen reranker losses and a dozen sparse losses, all feeding one Hugging Face Trainer subclass so you get mixed precision, multi-GPU, and logging for free. Evaluation runs during training with eleven ready evaluators, hard negatives can be mined from any corpus with one function call, and trained models auto-generate full model cards for the Hub. That is a complete path from raw pairs to a searchable, shareable artifact.

The detailed map: family facades and their key methods, the BaseModel core with save, hub, cards, adapters, and modality handling, the module stack, the training bridge with losses and samplers, evaluators, and the utility and backend layer.

The cleanest place to understand this codebase is the inheritance diamond that is not. BaseModel at line 66 declares itself as nn.Sequential, PeftAdapterMixin, and ABC, which means a model instance is simultaneously the module chain, a loadable adapter host, and a family contract. Its 2045 lines carry the universal verbs: save_pretrained at 806 walks the module chain and serializes each module’s config and state, push_to_hub at 950 packages the folder with the model card machinery from a 2052-line model_card.py, and the 941-line modality.py defines how text, image, audio, and video inputs are named, processed, and routed. The Router at line 30 picks the right input module per modality, which is how the CLIP module and the text Transformer coexist in one framework.

The family facades then differentiate on output shape. SentenceTransformer’s encode at 753 is the single-vector path, with encode_multi_process at 1101 for corpus-scale jobs and similarity at 1056 dispatching to cosine, dot, euclidean, or manhattan. CrossEncoder’s predict at 450 feeds pairs through the transformer and a scoring head, and rank at 642 wraps predict with sorting so the README’s three-passage Berlin query returns corpus ids, scores, and texts in order, with the ms-marco MiniLM checkpoint printing 8.61, 6.35, and 5.51 for its three candidates. SparseEncoder’s encode at 578 produces a vector the width of the vocabulary, and its static sparsity method at 1157 reports what the README demonstrates on a SPLADE model: ninety-nine point eight percent of activations are zero. MultiVectorEncoder splits into encode_query at 355 and encode_document at 531, then scores with MaxSim at 977, where each query token picks its best-matching document token, which is why the README example encodes a ten-token query into a 10 by 128 matrix and scores a Paris document at 9.60 against a Berlin one at 9.41.

Training is deliberately boring in the best way. SentenceTransformerTrainer is only 168 lines at line 36 because the 1334-line BaseTrainer at line 89 already extends the Hugging Face Trainer with column remapping, multi-dataset sampling through an 806-line sampler, and a 187-line collator that pairs texts with labels. The loss libraries are where the research lives: the CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss at line 26 is one of twenty-eight embedding losses, caching gradient-safe negatives so contrastive training scales without OOM. The legacy fit method survives at line 160 of fit_mixin.py as a compatibility path that compiles old-style arguments into the trainer stack.

The last mile is deployment and data, and both get real code rather than afterthoughts. mine_hard_negatives at line 25 of a 948-line module scans a corpus with an existing model to manufacture difficult negatives, the single highest-leverage trick for embedding quality. quantization.py compresses embeddings to binary and scalar forms across 564 lines for cheaper indexes. And the backend layer loads ONNX models at line 14 and OpenVINO at 92, with export helpers for optimized ONNX at optimize.py line 19, dynamic ONNX quantization at quantize.py line 24, and static OpenVINO quantization at line 109, so a trained model leaves Python behind without leaving the framework.

From Install to Embeddings

The stack asks for Python 3.10 or newer, PyTorch 2.2 or newer, and transformers v5 or newer:

pip install -U sentence-transformers

Then the canonical example from the repository’s README:

from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

model = SentenceTransformer("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

sentences = [
    "The weather is lovely today.",
    "It's so sunny outside!",
    "He drove to the stadium.",
]
embeddings = model.encode(sentences)
print(embeddings.shape)
# => (3, 384)

similarities = model.similarity(embeddings, embeddings)
print(similarities)
# tensor([[1.0000, 0.6660, 0.1046],
#         [0.6660, 1.0000, 0.1411],
#         [0.1046, 0.1411, 1.0000]])

Three sentences become three 384-dimensional vectors, and one matrix multiplication answers which sentences mean the same thing. Swap the class name for CrossEncoder, SparseEncoder, or MultiVectorEncoder and the same four-line shape serves reranking, sparse search, or late interaction, with the repo even shipping an agent skill, installable via hf skills add train-sentence-transformers, that lets coding agents drive the training APIs directly.

Honest limits: the four-family breadth is new, and the seams show in version churn, with the jump to Trainer-based training in v3 and the multimodal expansion still leaving deprecation trails that the codebase keeps politely shimming. The legacy fit path exists precisely because a decade of tutorials depends on it. Rerankers and late-interaction models are compute-hungry at query time, and the library will not make a CrossEncoder cheap, only easy. Sparse and multi-vector support, while first-class, leans on a smaller model zoo than the dense family. And the module-chain design, elegant as it is, means a model directory is a contract: load a chain you did not build and you inherit its preprocessing decisions. Still, the core achievement stands: one import gives you four decades-worth of retrieval research in a shape you can actually ship, which is why sentence-transformers remains the default answer to how do I embed text.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of UKPLab/sentence-transformers: how SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder, SparseEncoder, and MultiVectorEncoder share one BaseModel of composable modules, one HF Trainer bridge, and one set of similarity utilities to serve dense, reranked, sparse, and late-interaction retrieval.

entry.title: FP8 Without Rewriting Your Stack - Inside NVIDIA/TransformerEngine

link.title: FP8 Without Rewriting Your Stack - Inside NVIDIA/TransformerEngine

entry.content:
Training large models in FP8 promises roughly double the throughput and half the memory traffic of BF16, and the 2022 paper FP8 Formats for Deep Learning is the reason the industry believes it. The catch has always been numerics: eight-bit formats have tiny dynamic ranges, so every matmul needs scale factors, running maximums, and careful bookkeeping, and hand-rolling that across a transformer is a research project of its own. NVIDIA/TransformerEngine, the Apache-2.0 library behind FP8 training in Megatron-LM, NeMo, Hugging Face Accelerate, Lightning, and Amazon SageMaker, is the industrial answer: version 2.19, released in September 2026, carries FP8 recipes for Hopper through Rubin silicon plus MXFP8 and NVFP4 block scaling for Blackwell, fused kernels for attention, GEMMs, norms, and MoE, and a two-line API that hides all of it. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

The repository splits into four packages: common holds the recipe definitions shared by every framework, pytorch is the 137-file flagship, jax mirrors the API across fifty files, and debug is a twenty-one-file numerics debugger. The design principle is separation of policy from mechanism. Recipes in common declare what precision policy you want; an autocast context manager in pytorch/quantization.py applies it region by region; a family of quantized tensor types carries the actual scaled data through the graph; and fused modules, from a plain Linear to a full TransformerLayer, call kernels that consume that data natively. Reading the overview from left to right traces one forward pass from recipe selection to quantized math to distributed infrastructure.

Overview of TransformerEngine: a shared recipe family feeds fp8_autocast, which quantizes work through fused modules into a QuantizedTensor contract implemented by Float8, MXFP8, and NVFP4 types, all resting on distributed and MoE infrastructure with a mirrored JAX API.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Recipe family is the policy base at line 110, with DelayedScaling at 176, Float8CurrentScaling at 289, MXFP8BlockScaling at 345, and NVFP4BlockScaling at 502.
  • fp8_autocast at line 980 of a 2044-line module is the context manager that switches quantizers on when you enter a region.
  • TransformerEngineBaseModule at line 948 is the contract every fused module extends.
  • Linear at line 1904 of 1904-plus lines wraps its custom autograd function at 1807 for FP8 GEMMs.
  • LayerNormMLP at line 2156 fuses normalization with the gated MLP block so intermediate activations stay in low precision.
  • DotProductAttention at line 594 dispatches fused attention across supported backends.
  • QuantizedTensor defines the storage at line 54 and the Quantizer ABC at 371 that every format implements.
  • distributed.py is the 2271-line infrastructure file with activation recomputation at 241 and an RNG state tracker at 832.

Why You Need This

The first reason is that low precision is a moving target that no application wants to chase alone. In three years the field went from delayed-scaling FP8 on Hopper to per-tensor current scaling, to MXFP8 microscaling blocks, to NVFP4 four-bit training on Blackwell, with hybrid quantization and FP8 attention support arriving release by release. Each format has different scale layouts, kernel requirements, and numerics traps. TransformerEngine absorbs that churn behind one recipe interface, so moving your training from FP8 to MXFP8 is changing a constructor argument, not rewriting quantization logic across your model.

The second reason is integration depth with the frameworks you already use. The autocast API is deliberately shaped like torch.autocast, so adopting it is a wrapper around the forward pass rather than a restructure. Megatron-LM uses it for tensor, sequence, context, and expert parallelism with communication overlap; Accelerate and Lightning expose it as precision plugins; SageMaker’s model parallel library builds on the same primitives. Even better, the pytorch and jax packages share the recipe definitions in common, so a numerics decision made once applies to both ecosystems, and the JAX side ships its own dropless MoE path tuned for GB200-class systems. The attention package even carries inference plumbing, with a KVCacheManager at line 21 of attention/inference.py and a paged variant at 596, so the same library serves decode-time serving and training-time throughput.

The third reason is that the library treats fused kernels and quantization as one problem, not two. A naive FP8 implementation quantizes weights and activations, runs a fast GEMM, then pays the savings back in elementwise glue. The modules here fuse the glue into the kernels: LayerNormLinear folds the norm into the GEMM epilogue, LayerNormMLP keeps the entire norm-plus-expansion block in low precision, GroupedLinear batches expert weights into single calls, and the attention stack dispatches to fused backends including FP8 attention. CUDA graph support in a 1735-line graph.py then captures the steady state so launch overhead disappears at scale. Throughput comes from the whole chain, and the whole chain is here.

The detailed map: the recipe hierarchy and autocast region manager, the fused module family, the quantized tensor zoo, MoE routing and permutation, runtime infrastructure from CUDA graphs to fused optimizers, and the JAX mirror with debugging tools.

The recipe layer is the policy brain, and it is refreshingly small. Recipe at line 110 is a dataclass-style base, and the four public strategies are subclasses in the same file: DelayedScaling at 176 tracks amax history over a window and is the classic Hopper-era recipe; Float8CurrentScaling at 289 computes scales from the current step’s maximums; MXFP8BlockScaling at 345 and NVFP4BlockScaling at 502 encode Blackwell’s hardware microscaling formats. Policy objects carry no tensors; they are declarative. The mechanism lives in quantization.py, which opens by probing hardware support with functions like check_fp8_support at 191, then provides fp8_model_init at 886 so parameters are born ready for quantization, and fp8_autocast at 980, which on entry pushes the recipe’s quantizers into a global manager and on exit restores the previous state. The QuantizerRole and QuantizerRequest types at lines 59 and 117 make the handoff explicit.

The quantized tensor zoo is where formats become data. QuantizedTensorStorage at line 54 holds the raw bytes and scale planes, and the Quantizer ABC at 371 defines the quantize and dequantize contract. Each format then gets its own file: Float8Tensor at line 440 with its current-scaling quantizer at 197, Float8BlockwiseQTensor at 258 of the blockwise file, plus MXFP8 and NVFP4 siblings in their own modules, and a HybridTensor and GroupedTensor for mixed and batched cases. Two functions in quantized_tensor.py, prepare_for_saving at 291 and restore_from_saved at 318, manage the awkward autograd moment when quantized activations must be stashed for backward without defeating the memory savings that motivated them.

The fused modules are the biggest files in the package and the least negotiable to hand-write. TransformerEngineBaseModule at 948 centralizes weight initialization, quantization mode selection, and reset mechanics. Linear reaches line 1904 because its autograd function at 1807 must handle every combination of quantized and unquantized inputs, weight caching, and gradient accumulation in FP8. LayerNormLinear at 1546 and LayerNormMLP at 2156 push fusion further, and GroupedLinear at 1605 exists for MoE, where dozens of expert GEMMs must batch into few kernel launches. On top sit DotProductAttention at 594, a torch-compatible MultiheadAttention at 48 of multi_head_attention.py, and the TransformerLayer at line 71 that assembles the canonical block with DropPath at 46.

The MoE and infrastructure layers round out the system. Token routing lives in a 561-line router.py, expert placement and collectives in a 1245-line ep.py, and the token sort-and-unsort dance in permutation.py’s 1347 lines, all exposed through an operation graph whose dispatch and combine operations sit in the 38-file ops package. Around everything, distributed.py provides activation recomputation at 241 and deterministic RNG tracking at 832, cpu_offload.py moves state to host memory across 944 lines with a 751-line v1 variant kept for compatibility, and the fused optimizers package ships fused Adam, SGD, and multi-tensor apply. The JAX mirror keeps the same recipe objects and adds its own fp8_autocast at line 814 of jax/quantize/helper.py. A 21-file debug package, wired through debug/init.py, rounds it out with buffers and hooks for inspecting exactly what the quantizers did to your tensors, which is the difference between guessing at a loss spike and reading it.

From Install to FP8 Training

The package builds from source against your CUDA toolchain, so the README recommends no-build-isolation and prebuilt NGC containers:

pip install --no-build-isolation "transformer_engine[pytorch]"
# or, in a ready environment:
docker run --gpus all -it --rm nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:YY.MM-py3

The canonical usage is a context manager around the forward pass, straight from the project’s getting-started flow:

import torch
import transformer_engine.pytorch as te
from transformer_engine.common.recipe import DelayedScaling

linear = te.Linear(768, 3072, bias=True)

recipe = DelayedScaling()
with te.fp8_autocast(enabled=True, fp8_recipe=recipe):
    out = linear(torch.randn(16, 128, 768, device="cuda"))

Inside the context, the Linear’s weights and the input quantize through the active recipe, the GEMM runs on FP8 tensor cores, and scales update automatically. Swap DelayedScaling for Float8CurrentScaling, MXFP8BlockScaling, or NVFP4BlockScaling and the same two lines address three generations of hardware formats.

Honest limits: the hardware floor is real. FP8 needs Hopper or newer, MXFP8 and NVFP4 need Blackwell, and on Ampere you get FP16 and BF16 optimizations only, so the library is exactly as universal as NVIDIA’s product line. Building from source ties you to specific CUDA, cuDNN, and PyTorch version combinations, which is why the NGC container is the advertised path rather than a convenience. The JAX API, while sharing recipes, is a separate surface with its own maturity curve. Debugging low-precision numerics stays genuinely hard; the debug package helps, but scale-factor bugs still look like mysterious loss spikes. And the abstraction rewards standard architectures: highly custom blocks may fall back to unquantized paths silently. None of this dims the achievement, which is making an eight-bit world navigable with a context manager, and doing it for both of the frameworks that matter.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of NVIDIA/TransformerEngine: how recipes, an autocast region manager, a family of quantized tensors, fused modules from Linear to TransformerLayer, and expert-parallel MoE machinery put FP8, MXFP8, and NVFP4 training behind a one-line context manager for PyTorch and JAX.

entry.title: The Engine That Sharded BLOOM - Inside microsoft/DeepSpeed

link.title: The Engine That Sharded BLOOM - Inside microsoft/DeepSpeed

entry.content:
When Microsoft’s AI at Scale initiative committed to training language models measured in hundreds of billions of parameters, the binding constraint was not model design but memory arithmetic. A 176-billion-parameter model in mixed precision needs hundreds of gigabytes just to hold its weights, and several times more once optimizer states and gradients join the party. DeepSpeed is the open-source training system Microsoft built to break that wall, and its track record is written into the repository’s own README: Megatron-Turing NLG at 530 billion parameters, BLOOM at 176 billion, Jurassic-1 at 178 billion, YaLM at 100 billion, GPT-NeoX at 20 billion, and Turing NLG at 17 billion all passed through this engine. The whole system ships under the Apache 2.0 license, which means every trick that made those runs fit is sitting in plain sight in the source tree.

What surprises first-time readers is how much of the system lives in plain Python. Beneath a thin layer of fused CUDA kernels, DeepSpeed is an orchestrator: a launcher that SSHes into your cluster, an engine class that re-implements the training loop with sharded bookkeeping, three ZeRO stages that progressively cut memory, a pipe-parallel subsystem, an autotuner, and a hardware abstraction that now speaks NVIDIA, AMD, Ascend, Gaudi, Intel XPU, and plain CPU. Reading it teaches you how modern distributed training actually works, one hook and one partition at a time. As always in this series, what follows is an educational tour of published source code.

DeepSpeed overview: two entry points feed the DeepSpeedEngine, which drives the ZeRO stages, pipe and MoE parallelism, and a platform layer of collectives, accelerator backends, and JIT-compiled ops.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • the initialize() entry point — one call that wraps a plain PyTorch model and a JSON config into a managed distributed engine.
  • the launcher runner — parses a hostfile into a resource pool and fans out training processes across machines over SSH.
  • DeepSpeedEngine — the 5,153-line heart of the library where forward, backward, and step acquire their distributed meaning.
  • ZeRO stage 1 and 2 — partitions optimizer states and gradients across data-parallel ranks.
  • ZeRO stage 3 — shards the parameters themselves, with CPU and NVMe offload in the ZeRO-Infinity style.
  • partition_parameters.py — the zero.Init machinery that builds models no single rank can hold.
  • the pipe engine — layer-split parallelism driven by micro-batch schedules across a process topology.
  • the JIT op builder — a registry of fused kernels compiled on first use through ninja.

Why You Need This

The first reason is practical: the memory wall is the wall you hit. Train anything past a few billion parameters on commodity GPUs and PyTorch’s default data-parallel replicate-everything model stops fitting long before your compute does. ZeRO’s insight, implemented in three escalating stages, is that a training cluster wastes staggering amounts of memory by keeping identical optimizer states on every rank. Stage one partitions those states, stage two adds gradient partitioning, and stage three goes all the way and partitions the model parameters, gathering each layer on the fly only for the instants it is needed. When even stage three is not enough, the offload machinery spills states and parameters to CPU memory or NVMe storage, which is how a machine with modest GPUs can co-author a 176-billion-parameter run.

The second reason is the engineering itself. This codebase is a masterclass in the unglamorous systems work that papers skip: a prefetch coordinator that issues asynchronous parameter fetches before a layer needs them, a contiguous memory allocator that packs fragmented shards into bandwidth-friendly flat buffers, a tiling module that slices single enormous layers so they can pass through a sharded step, and a swap layer that moves optimizer state asynchronously so the GPU never stalls waiting for storage. None of these ideas is exotic in isolation, but seeing them composed inside one coherent engine is the difference between reading the ZeRO papers and understanding them.

The third reason is leverage. The abstractions pioneered here became the default vocabulary of the field: Hugging Face Transformers, Accelerate, PyTorch Lightning, MosaicML Composer, Determined, and MMEngine all ship DeepSpeed integrations, and the research has kept moving with DeepSpeed-MoE, ZeRO++, Ulysses sequence parallelism, ZenFlow, SuperOffload, and DeepCompile arriving year after year. If you work with large models in any capacity, the patterns in this tree — partitioned parameters, hook-driven offload, schedule-driven collectives — reappear everywhere from inference servers to fine-tuning frameworks, and recognizing them by name makes every other system easier to read.

The detailed view: launcher and collectives at the top, the ZeRO internals block with its offload and prefetch machinery, the pipe-parallel subsystem, training support modules, and the platform layer underneath.

Start where every user starts: deepspeed/runtime/engine.py. The file runs to 5,153 lines, and the class DeepSpeedEngine opens at line 516 after a long module-level initialize() function has already read your config JSON and made the load-bearing decisions. From there the engine is a conventional training loop wearing a distributed coat: forward begins at line 2987, backward at 3386, the optimizer step at 3571, and checkpointing at save_checkpoint (line 4873) and load_checkpoint (line 4399), with train and eval entry points near lines 2887 and 2893. Along the way the engine wires in a timer module for the wallclock breakdowns you see in logs, and a small monitor dispatcher that routes metrics to TensorBoard, WandB, or CSV depending on your config. The elegance is that the user’s training script never changes shape — the engine intercepts the same three calls and adds bookkeeping between them.

The ZeRO block is where the memory actually gets saved. stage_1_and_2.py, at 3,464 lines, implements DeepSpeedZeroOptimizer: it flattens gradients, reduces and partitions them by rank, and hands the update to a fused optimizer — fused_optimizer.py, 456 lines, keeps FP16 master weights in a single flat buffer updated by one kernel call. Stage three is a different beast entirely. stage3.py, 3,435 lines, registers every parameter as a partition, and its companion partition_parameters.py, 2,093 lines, provides the zero.Init context so a model can be constructed from the start without any rank materializing the full weights. The runtime choreography lives in parameter_offload.py (552 lines), which pushes parameters to CPU or NVMe and swaps them back ahead of each forward and backward, and partitioned_param_coordinator.py (587 lines), which peeks at upcoming module executions to issue asynchronous prefetches so gathers overlap with compute. Supporting cast includes contiguous_memory_allocator.py for flat buffers, tiling.py (230 lines) for layers too big for one sharded pass, offload_states.py (87 lines) as a scoped context that lends the GPU to another workload, and a partitioned optimizer swapper in swap_tensor that moves states without blocking the step.

Parallelism beyond data-parallel lives in two places. The pipe subsystem mirrors a miniature framework: pipe/engine.py (1,153 lines) subclasses DeepSpeedEngine and buffers micro-batches, module.py (580 lines) lets you declare which layers live on which stage, schedule.py (486 lines) encodes the clock-cycle choreography of forwards, backwards, and buffer exchanges, topology.py (378 lines) models the process mesh where data, pipe, and model-parallel axes intersect, and p2p.py (136 lines) supplies the raw send and recv. Alongside it, sharded_moe.py (635 lines) implements DeepSpeed-MoE’s top-K expert routing with capacity-aware dispatch, and module_inject (replace_module.py at 632 lines plus a 26-line policy base) can swap standard transformer blocks for optimized kernels at load time. Combine data, pipe, and tensor axes and you get the 3D parallelism that carried the 530-billion-parameter runs.

Two subsystems make all of this operable. The launcher splits into launch.py (250 lines), the command-line front door, and runner.py (523 lines), which reads a hostfile into a resource pool, checks each host’s reachability over SSH, and honors a no-SSH mode for single-box runs — it is the piece that turns one command into a synchronized cluster. The autotuner (autotuner.py at 957 lines with a 352-line scheduler) runs training trials over a search space of ZeRO stages, offload targets, and micro-batch sizes, scores them with an exponential-median scheme, and writes the winning configuration back for production use. Underneath everything, the accelerator package defines a 326-line abstract device contract with concrete implementations for CUDA, CPU, Intel XPU, Ascend NPU, HPU for Gaudi, Apple MPS, and more, while comm.py (818 lines) wraps the collectives with timing hooks and a oneCCL backend so even CPU-only clusters can participate. The op builder registry, 839 lines, JIT-compiles the fused kernels on first use through ninja and torch’s extension machinery, caching results so the compile cost is paid once.

The research frontier is unusually visible in the tree. superoffload_stage3.py (320 lines) implements the SuperOffload engine for superchip hardware that earned an ASPLOS 2026 honorable mention; a zenflow package carries the stall-free offloading engine from its 2025 write-up; inference v2 has its own engine module. Recent news items trace the pace: Muon optimizer support and SDMA offloaded collectives for AMD GPUs landed in May 2026, a core API update in December 2025 added PyTorch-style backward hooks and low-precision master states, and ZeRO++ powered large-scale distillation for recommendation models at LinkedIn. Arctic Long Sequence Training pushed context windows into the millions of tokens, DeepNVMe made NVMe bandwidth a first-class citizen, and DeepCompile and AutoTP brought compiler-style and automatic tensor-parallel optimizations into the mix. The repository doubles as a living index of systems-for-ML research.

From Install to First Sharded Step

Installation is one pip command, and the ops compile on demand:

pip install deepspeed
ds_report
deepspeed --num_gpus=4 train.py --deepspeed_config ds_config.json

The ds_report command prints which compiled kernels are available and which will be built on first use, which is invaluable for debugging environments. Your training script changes by three lines: import deepspeed, wrap the model with deepspeed.initialize, and hand a JSON config that names the ZeRO stage and offload targets. A minimal stage-two config with CPU optimizer offload is a dozen lines of JSON. On Windows the project offers a build_win.bat script for pre-building, with a documented caveat that the asynchronous I/O and GDS offload backends are unsupported there. The launcher accepts a hostfile listing one hostname per line with slot counts, and from that moment your four-GPU workstation and your twelve-node cluster are driven by the same command.
